title: S-Row — さ し す せ そ

points.name: さ
points.explanation: The syllable さ combines an 's' consonant with the vowel あ, producing a clear 'sa' sound exactly as in 'saga' or 'salsa'. Japanese 's' is a straightforward fricative — similar to English — so さ is one of the easier sounds in this row. You'll encounter さ all the time: it appears in さかな (fish), さけ (sake / salmon), and in the common filler word さあ ('well...' or 'hmm...') that Japanese speakers use while thinking. The character さ has a distinctive looping shape that many learners find memorable.
rules: The 's' is a clean fricative, very similar to English — no major adjustments needed.
Follow directly with the open 'ah' vowel without a pause.
さ is written in three strokes: two horizontal lines crossed by a curved vertical, then a separate curved stroke.

points.name: し
points.explanation: The syllable し is the most irregular sound in the S-row: instead of a plain 'si', it produces a 'shi' sound — exactly like the 'she' in English 'she' or 'shiver'. This is not a mistake or exception; it's simply how Japanese evolved, and し follows this pattern consistently every time. English speakers generally have no trouble with this sound since 'sh' is very natural. し appears in an enormous number of common Japanese words: し alone can mean 'four', 'poetry', or 'death' depending on context (another reminder that pitch accent matters in Japanese!).
rules: Always pronounced 'shi' — never 'si'. This is one of the fixed irregularities of the S-row.
The 'sh' is a retroflex fricative, same as in English 'she' — no special technique needed.
し looks like a fishhook curving to the right — a shape many learners use as a memory aid.

points.name: す
points.explanation: The syllable す combines 's' with the Japanese vowel う, producing a sound like 'su' — but remember that Japanese う is unrounded, so this sounds slightly different from English 'sue' or 'soup'. In natural, fast Japanese speech, the う in す is often devoiced (nearly silent) when it appears between voiceless consonants or at the end of a word — for example, the common polite verb ending ます is often heard more like 'mas' than 'masu'. This devoicing is a hallmark of natural Japanese speech, but don't worry about producing it deliberately yet.
rules: The 's' is identical to English — a clean fricative.
The う is unrounded: flat lips, not pushed forward like in 'sue'.
In casual speech, final す often devoices (the vowel becomes very faint) — you'll hear this constantly in verbs ending in ます.

points.name: せ
points.explanation: The syllable せ pairs 's' with the vowel え, making a clean 'se' sound like the beginning of 'set' or 'settle'. This is one of the more straightforward hiragana syllables — the 's' and 'e' both function very similarly to their English counterparts. せ appears in important everyday vocabulary, including せかい (world), せき (cough / seat), and せんせい (teacher — one of the first words most Japanese students learn). The character せ is sometimes compared to the English letter 'E' rotated or simplified.
rules: Clean 's' consonant followed by a pure 'eh' vowel — very natural for English speakers.
Don't let the vowel drift toward 'ay'; keep it a short, clean 'e' as in 'bed'.
せ appears in せんせい (teacher) and せかい (world) — two high-frequency words worth memorizing early.

points.name: そ
points.explanation: The syllable そ combines 's' with the vowel お, making a 'so' sound like the start of 'soul' or 'sofa'. Japanese speakers keep the vowel clean and brief, without the English glide toward 'w' at the end. そ is an incredibly useful syllable because it's the basis of the 'that/those' demonstrative series: そ points to things near the listener (そこ 'there', それ 'that thing', その 'that'). You'll hear and use these demonstratives within your very first conversations in Japanese.
rules: Clean 's' plus a pure 'oh' vowel — stop before the lips start gliding toward 'w'.
そ is the root of そこ (there), それ (that), and その (that) — useful pointing words.
The character そ has one or two strokes depending on the typeface — both are correct.

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this character make?
chapterPractice.explanation: し makes the 'shi' sound (like 'she'), not 'si'. This is one of the irregular sounds in the S-row — it always says 'shi'.
す makes the 'su' sound. Remember that the vowel is unrounded — lips stay flat, not pushed forward like in English 'sue'.
いす (isu) means 'chair'. い (i) + す (su) = isu. A classic beginner vocabulary word!
そこ (soko) means 'there', specifically a place near the listener. そ (so) + こ (ko) — the そ series points toward the listener's space.
